A 44-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of headache, dizziness, and imbalance. He had a history of hypertension and cervical disc herniation. One year ago, he underwent transcatheter closure for patent foramen ovale. annotation_jobs.vignette:
A man in his 80s was brought to the emergency department after a cardiac arrest. According to paramedics, the patient was last seen healthy by his family 4 hours earlier, then was found unresponsive and pulseless in the bathroom. He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, receiving 4 doses of epinephrine intravenously and endotracheal tube intubation with return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 10 minutes. Family later revealed he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and had been complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation. A family member witnessed him struggling for air before losing consciousness.

Initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity.

- ECG findings:    - Sinus rhythm at approximately 100 beats per minute    - Right axis deviation    - Prolonged QRS duration with rsR' complexes in lead V1    - Wide S waves in leads I and V6    - Prolonged r to peak R' time in lead V1    - QT interval of 360 ms measurable in leads V4-V6    - QRS duration of 133 ms in inferior leads  - Coronary angiography:    No acute occlusions found  Image Title: Figure 1. 12-Lead Electrocardiogram at Presentation  Image Title: Figure 2. Inferior and Lateral Leads From Repeated Electrocardiogram Demonstrating Discernible T Waves  Image Title: Figure 3. Leads II, III, V5, and V6 of Initial Electrocardiogram

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A man in his 60s presented with a 3-month history of intertrigo involving his groin that he had been treating with a combination of clotrimazole cream, 1%, and hydrocortisone cream, 1%. The condition improved, but he then developed bright red, burning and painful nodules around his scrotum. Medical history included prostate cancer, hypertension, anxiety disorder, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and diverticulosis. Current medications included omeprazole, alprazolam, amlodipine besylate, atenolol, simvastatin, and valsartan.

Two symmetrical solitary erythematous nodules were present in the right and left inguinal folds adjacent to the scrotum.

She had recently undergone tricuspid valve replacement with a 29-mm bioprosthetic Carpentier-Edwards valve complicated by transient third-degree heart block. Two days after pacemaker placement, she experienced episodes of light-headedness and chest pain.

Blood pressure was 94/60 mm Hg. Heart rates were between 150 and 190 beats per minute.

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with new and progressive satellite lesions while undergoing pembrolizumab therapy. Two years earlier, he had undergone a wide local excision with graft repair for a left posterior auricular scalp lesion. An incidentally resected lymph node was found to be focally involved, with no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Within months, multiple unresectable satellite lesions appeared. He received 4 cycles of ipilimumab, followed by a second wide local excision when new lesions appeared. Additional satellite lesions developed and he began pembrolizumab therapy, but after 5 cycles, local progression occurred in the satellite lesions.

Multiple satellite lesions were present on the left posterior auricular scalp area. After treatment, clinically regressed lesions with persistent black pigmentation were noted.

A 61-year-old man with a medical history of factor V Leiden mutation (discovered after an episode of abdominal venous thromboembolism), hypothyroidism, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus, and four transient ischemic attacks. annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 63-year-old woman presented with difficult-to-treat hypertension. Medical history included bone and central diabetes insipidus diagnosed via femoral biopsy 12 years ago, and liver involvement three years prior that was treated with cytarabine for one year. The patient had untreated dyslipidemia (LDL cholesterol 3.11 mmol/L). She was not a smoker and did not have diabetes. Her body mass index was 19.22 kg/m². No relevant family history was reported. The patient did not report angina, exertional dyspnea, or claudication.

Blood pressure was 198/106 mmHg without orthostatic hypotension or anisosphygmia, and heart rate was 65 beats/min. The cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and a continuous murmur was heard in the epigastric region.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Serum creatinine: 96.36 μmol/L (1.09 mg/dL)    * Potassium: 4.4 mmol/L    * B-type natriuretic peptide: 82,500 pg/mL    * Inflammatory markers: normal    * Urinalysis: unremarkable without albuminuria  - Imaging Studies:    * Transthoracic echocardiogram: left ventricular mass index of 110 g/m² without other relevant changes    * Abdominal CT angiogram:      Title: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT      Description: Right kidney atrophy without discernible right renal artery and high-grade ostial stenosis of the left renal, celiac trunk, and superior mesenteric arteries    * Diethylenetriamine pentaacetate renogram: confirmed right kidney functional exclusion    * Renal vein catheterization: no signs of renin production lateralization

A 71-year-old man presented with three weeks of jaundice, weight loss, abdominal pain, and dark-colored urine. He also reported bilateral lower-extremity weakness that was most noticeable when attempting to arise from a chair, resulting in several ground-level falls. He had no history of autoimmune or neuromuscular conditions. Despite his recent falls, he did not have any prolonged periods of being down that could contribute to muscle injury. He had been taking atorvastatin as a home medication.

Physical findings included:- Jaundice and significant scleral icterus- Epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound- Mild weakness in bilateral hip flexor muscles

Laboratory Results:- Aspartate aminotransferase: 2536 IU/L- Alanine aminotransferase: 919 IU/L  - Total bilirubin: 169.3 μmol/L- Alkaline phosphatase: 894 IU/L- Creatinine: 415.5 μmol/L (baseline of 70.7 μmol/L three months previously)- Initial creatinine kinase (CK) level: 22,000 IU/L, later peaked at >40,000 IU/L- Cancer antigen 19-9 level: 2930 kU/LImaging Studies:- CT abdomen/pelvis: 2.6 × 3.1 cm pancreatic head mass with associated pancreatic ductal dilatation, without evidence of metastatic disease- MRI: Diffuse myositis affecting lower extremities  Image Description: Axial and coronal views showing diffuse symmetrical hyperintense signal highly suggestive of diffuse myositisPathology:- Pancreatic head biopsy: Hypocellular with scant atypical cells- Biliary stricture biopsy: Consistent with adenocarcinoma- Right biceps femoris biopsy: Nonspecific myopathic changes consistent with rhabdomyolysis- BiliSeq genetic sequencing: Demonstrated genomic alterations in targeted regions of genes involved in biliary-tract malignancies

Patient was tachycardic, diaphoretic, and febrile. Several areas of skin over his face, chest, and abdomen showed hardened plaque and depigmentation. Over the upper extremities, hardened nodules of varying sizes were noted, along with larger hardened masses that were fixed and nontender to palpation. The right foot/ankle was fluctuant and tender to palpation.

Laboratory Results:
- Normal renal function
- Leukocytosis (WBC count: 18.7 × 10³/UL)
- Elevated total creatine kinase (1947 U/L)
- Normal corrected calcium (9.62 mg/dL)
- Depressed phosphorus (1.7 mg/dL)
- Normal lactic acid (1.7 mmol/L) and magnesium (1.9 mg/dL)

Imaging Studies:
- X-ray sagittal view of right lower extremity
  Image Description: Showed soft tissue calcifications unrelated to bone or cartilage, negative for osteomyelitis or subcutaneous gas
- CT scan of right lower extremity
  Image Description: Sagittal view at the level of the cuboid and fibular malleolus showing soft tissue calcifications

Pathology:
- Findings confirmed calcified tissue with inflamed stroma and necrosis

What is the most likely diagnosis?

annotation_jobs.vignette:
An 84-year-old man with a medical history of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and tobacco use was admitted for evaluation of an asymptomatic abdominal mass with pulsations. The patient had a 20-pack-year smoking history and had been smoking pipe tobacco for the past 10 years. The patient did not report shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, lower extremity weakness, or abdominal, back, or chest pain. A previous scan 9 years prior showed the mass was 3 cm.

Vital signs: Temperature - afebrile, Blood pressure - 120/76 mm Hg, Pulse rate - 73 beats/min, Respiratory rate - 16/minute. Examination revealed a well-defined large pulsatile mass palpable in the epigastric region with a soft bruit audible on auscultation. Pulses were palpable in the lower extremities bilaterally.

- Laboratory tests: Complete blood count and electrolyte levels were within normal limits.

- Imaging Studies:
  1. Computed tomographic angiogram (CTA) of abdomen and pelvis:
    Image Title: Figure 1 - CTA Abdomen and Pelvis
    Image Description: (A) Axial view showing a saccular aneurysm measuring 14.6 cm × 12.6 cm in greatest transaxial dimension. (B) Sagittal view showing 14.7 cm craniocaudal dimension. The right ureter was significantly displaced anterolaterally. Dense calcifications of iliac vessels present without narrowing. No signs of impending rupture. Aneurysmal neck angulation greater than 60 degrees with neck tortuosity noted.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 52-year-old Caucasian man presented with septic shock and bilateral lower extremity soft-tissue wounds. Medical history includes alcohol use disorder and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (hemoglobin A1c of 7.5%). The patient had no history or findings suggestive of cirrhosis and had not traveled outside Southern California.

Patient presented with bilateral lower extremity soft-tissue wounds. Additional physical examination details were not provided in the case report.

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 59-year-old Japanese man presented with malaise and chills that began the day before his visit. Medical history included hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Four months prior, he was diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and had a history of perianal abscess during induction chemotherapy. The current admission was for maintenance chemotherapy with idarubicin and cytarabine. On day 10 of hospitalization, he experienced a 40.2°C fever, chills, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain when breathing deeply or coughing.

Vital signs:- Blood pressure: 122/74 mm Hg- Heart rate: 109 beats/min (consistently tachycardic)- Respiratory rate: 24 breaths/min- Oxygen saturation: 98% on room airPhysical findings:- Percussion tenderness in the right upper quadrant- Remainder of examination unremarkable

Laboratory Tests:- Blood count: Leukocyte count 0.1 × 10⁹/L (50% neutrophils), Thrombocytes 11.0 × 10⁹/L, Hemoglobin 8.0 g/L- Liver function: Total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, Aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L, Alkaline phosphatase 1065 U/L, γ-Glutamyl transpeptidase 168 U/LImaging Studies:- Image Title: Abdominal CT scan- Image Description: Multiple, small, circumscribed, hypoattenuating lesions in the liver and spleenMicrobiological Studies:- Blood cultures: Positive for yeast after 30 hours- Gram staining: Revealed arthroconidia and hyphal fungi- Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar: Dry cottony colonies with frosted glass appearance- Molecular identification: D1/D2 26S rDNA and internal transcribed spacer region of rRNA gene analysis performed- Drug susceptibility testing: MIC values - voriconazole 0.25 μg/mL, micafungin 4.0 μg/mL

candidates.label: Acute coronary syndrome with early post-infarction pericarditis

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 52-year-old man presented with sudden, pressure-like, substernal chest pain that started at rest and radiated to the left jaw, associated with nausea, dyspnea, and diaphoresis. Symptoms began approximately 6 hours before arrival. Two hours after intervention, the patient reported a new onset of fever and worsening chest pain that was retrosternal and sharp in quality, but not affected by positional changes or exertion.

Initial examination: Patient was tachycardic, with no murmurs. No crackles were present on lung auscultation. Jugular venous pressure was normal. Follow-up examination: Temperature of 38.3°C, auscultation revealed a new pericardial friction rub located over the left sternal border.

- Laboratory Tests:
Initial troponin levels were 14 µg/L

- Imaging Studies:
1. Initial ECG showed ST-segment elevations in leads II, aVF, and V3-V5
2. Coronary angiography findings: acute thrombotic total occlusion of the mid-segment of the left anterior descending artery with TIMI 0 flow. Ventriculography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 55% to 60%
3. Second ECG: complete resolution of ST-segment elevation in V2-V3 with persistence of ST-segment elevation in II, III, aVF, and V4-V6 without reciprocal changes
4. Third ECG (24 hours later): diffuse ST-segment elevation on II, III, aVF, and V3-V5 accompanied by PR-segment depression in I and II and PR-segment elevation in aVR without reciprocal changes
5. Transthoracic echocardiogram: no evidence of pericardial effusion, no wall motion abnormalities, ejection fraction of 55% to 60%

annotation_jobs.vignette:
An 81-year-old man initially developed a cough, subjective fever, and shortness of breath. He was first treated with azithromycin for bronchitis, followed by levofloxacin after a right upper lobe infiltrate was found. His symptoms progressed despite antibiotics. Medical history includes coronary artery disease with coronary artery bypass (two years prior), atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c: 8.1%). He had spent time at a Northern Minnesota cabin but reported minimal outdoor exposure. Previous missionary work in Colombia ended two years before admission. Never smoked and rarely consumed alcohol.

Vital signs: Temperature 38.6°C, Pulse 130 beats/min, Blood Pressure 114/61 mm Hg, Respiratory Rate 22 breaths/min, Oxygen Saturation 82% (improved to >90% with 5 L/min oxygen). Lung sounds were diminished in the right upper lobe, with diffuse crackles in the right lung base. No clubbing or cyanosis. Cardiac examination showed tachycardic irregularly irregular rhythm, systolic ejection murmur, and mild pitting edema to the knee bilaterally. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Neurologic and skin examinations were normal. Later developed right-sided ptosis and anisocoria with an asymmetrically miotic right pupil (more evident in dark environment).

Laboratory Tests:
- Leukocytosis: 15,000/mm³
- Procalcitonin: 0.77 ng/mL
- Positive Blastomyces urine antigen
- Positive Histoplasmosis blood antigen
- Negative results for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
- Negative antigen tests for Cryptococcus, Legionella, and influenza
- Negative Paracoccidioides serum antibody

Imaging Studies:
1. Chest Radiograph
Title: Initial Chest Radiograph
Description: Dense consolidation of the right upper lobe, patchy nodular infiltrates of left upper lobe, 5-mm noncalcified rounded infiltrate in posterolateral left lower lobe

2. CT and MRI
Title: Emergency Head CT and Brain MRI
Description: Both showed no acute process

Other Tests:
Bronchoscopy findings: Moderate clear secretions with erythematous and edematous bronchial mucosa
Bronchoalveolar lavage: Spherical broadly based budding yeast on Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stain

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 35-year-old woman presented 11 weeks postpartum with right breast erythema and pain. She had experienced three prior episodes of similar symptoms treated at outside hospitals, with the most recent occurring at 9 weeks postpartum. Medical history includes depression and previous treatment with cabergoline until 2016. During her first trimester of pregnancy, hormone levels were normal. Postpartum, she continued to express an excessive amount of milk despite attempts to wean. No recurrent headaches or visual changes were reported. Her menstrual cycle had not resumed, and medications included multivitamins.

A 5 cm × 8 cm area of erythema and induration on the medial aspect of the right breast. No fluctuance was present, but a milky, nonpurulent discharge was easily expressed from both breasts.

Laboratory Tests:- Leukocyte count: 19.1 × 10⁹/L (normal: 4.5–11.0 × 10⁹/L)- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 33 mm/h (normal: 0–15 mm/h)- C-reactive protein: 11.8 mg/L (normal: <1 mg/L)- Thyroid-stimulating hormone: 1.429 mIU/L (normal: 0.55–4.78 mIU/L)- Prolactin: 72.3 ng/mL (normal: 4.8–23.3 ng/mL)- Anaerobic culture: Positive for Streptococcus agalactiae, susceptible to penicillinImaging Studies:- MRI Findings:  Title: Pituitary MRI  Description: Slightly heterogeneous appearance of the pituitary gland without evidence of discrete mass or lesion. No suprasellar mass or optic chiasm compression. Small areas of increased signal in the left frontal and right periarterial white matter.- Ultrasound Findings:  Title: Breast Ultrasound  Description: No abscess or focal lesion in the right breast.

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 54-year-old woman living in upstate New York with a medical history significant for idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia (ICL) originally diagnosed in 2015 with an annual CD4 cell count ranging between 14 and 18 cells/µL. She initially presented to her primary care physician with a sore throat. When symptoms did not improve after one week, she was referred to an otolaryngologist. The sore throat persisted despite a trial of omeprazole and fluctuated in intensity over the following months. Several months later, the patient began to experience dysphonia along with odynophagia. Throughout this course, the patient had no systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, myalgias) or pulmonary symptoms.

Laryngoscopy revealed thickening of the epiglottic mucosa with irregularity and white plaques. A repeat laryngoscopy demonstrated progression of the plaques.

- Laboratory Tests:
  * Laryngeal cultures initially grew Streptococcus mitis, Streptococcus salivarius, Rothia mucilaginosus, Neisseria flavescens/subflava, and Candida albicans
  * Urine histoplasma antigen: positive at 0.3 ng/mL
  * Acid-fast stain and culture: negative

- Imaging Studies:
  * Computed tomography of the chest revealed subtle ground-glass opacities in the left upper lobe

- Pathological Examination:
  * Laryngeal biopsy revealed rare hyphae and yeast forms on Grocott methenamine silver stain with no evidence of malignancy or granulomas
  * Fungal culture grew Histoplasma capsulatum, identified by typical tuberculate microconidia

- Images:
  * Figure 1 Title: Laryngoscopy findings
  * Figure 1 Description: Patient's epiglottis (A) and larynx (B) showing white plaques and thickening of the mucosa
  * Figure 2 Title: Microscopy findings
  * Figure 2 Description: (A) Mold with cottony texture and white-tan reverse after 16 days incubation, (B) Lactophenol cotton blue tease mount preparation showing large, thick-walled, round tuberculate macroconidia at 400× magnification

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presented with recurrent intense epigastric pain for 4-5 days. Episodes consisted of sudden burning pain in the epigastrium lasting 10-50 minutes, followed by nausea without emesis, and preceded by visual and auditory hallucinations. These episodes began 1 month after experiencing a severe COVID-19 infection that required ICU stay without respiratory support. annotation_jobs.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.

Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative.

- Histopathologic examination:    Image A: Clinical image of annular arc from a longitudinally furrowed skin lesion on the left eyebrow and forehead to an alopecic lesion    Image B: Clinical image of the bandlike grooved alopecic lesion on the left side of the frontal scalp and vertex    Image C: Scanning view shows predominant lymphocytic infiltrates in perifollicular and periappendageal regions of the dermis and lobular panniculitis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)    Image D: High-power view shows inflammatory infiltrates between adipocytes with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)  - Laboratory findings:    - Direct immunofluorescence: Positive with granular deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen in the dermal blood vessels    - Antinuclear antibody: Negative    - Antidouble-stranded DNA antibody: Negative    - All other laboratory test findings were normal

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 40-year-old man from eastern India presented with a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue present for the last 4 months. The lesion started as a small painless mass on the right lateral aspect of the tongue, which gradually grew and subsequently ulcerated. It caused mild difficulty in eating. No history of trauma or tongue bite preceding the lesion. Patient denied consuming tobacco or alcohol regularly. Medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for 2 years with oral hypoglycemic agents. No systemic complaints. No history of high-risk behavior for HIV.

Single well-defined ulcer measuring 2 × 2 cm on the right lateral aspect of tongue with a clean base and irregular and elevated heaped-up margins. No underlying induration, friability, or bleeding on manipulation. Rest of the oral cavity was normal.

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

A 47‐year‐old woman presented with crescendo chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath on exertion for two days. In the emergency department she was hypotensive, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Physical examination showed bilateral fine basal crepitations, a grade 2 decrescendo diastolic murmur, and bilateral pitting lower‐limb edema. She was an active smoker working in warehouse logistics, with no history of substance misuse or family history of cardiovascular disease.

Chest radiography demonstrated congested basal lung fields with mild bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment depressions in the inferior leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed anterior‐wall hypokinesia and moderate‐to‐severe aortic insufficiency; immobile echogenic shadows in the ascending aorta obscured the aortic valve. A computed tomography aortogram excluded aortic dissection. Urgent coronary angiography via the radial approach showed a slit-like left main coronary ostium while the remainder of the coronary arteries was free of atherosclerotic plaque.

These atypical findings prompted investigations for infectious and inflammatory aortitis. Potential causative organisms under consideration included Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella species, Staphylococcus species, and Campylobacter jejuni. Musculoskeletal examination and immunological assays were not suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or Behçet disease.

annotation_jobs.vignette:
A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

An 83-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive right mandibular pain radiating to the zygomatic and mastoid regions, requiring oxycodone, paracetamol, and ketorolac for relief. An empirical course of prednisone (50 mg per day) for presumed trigeminal neuralgia provided no benefit. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial CT showed enlargement of the right sphenoid sinus with overdevelopment and opacity of the lateral recess, bone thickening and sclerosis of the sphenoid walls, pterygoid process, and orbital apex, and focal interruption of the foramen rotundum and lateral recess wall. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated soft tissue protruding through a breach in the lateral recess wall of the sphenoid sinus, invading the right internal pterygoid muscles, masticatory and pterygopalatine fossae, and infiltrating the V2 and V3 trigeminal branches; intracranial extension into the cavernous sinus surrounded the Gasserian ganglion, with the cavernous carotid artery patent. T2-weighted images showed a markedly hypointense signal in the lateral recess with peripheral mucosal inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation revealed purulent discharge in the sphenoethmoidal recess. The patient underwent right endoscopic sinus surgery: after middle turbinectomy, the sphenoid ostium was obstructed by a pyocele, which was marsupialized and drained; samples of the lesion and surrounding mucosa were sent for bacteriological and histopathological examination. The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were then opened, the breach in the posterior-lateral sphenoid wall was repaired with mucoperiosteum, and a Merocel sponge was placed. He was discharged after 2 days without complications. Histopathology was negative for hyphae and neoplastic cells, and cultures grew no bacteria or fungi. One month after surgery, follow-up MRI confirmed persistent inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, skull base, and pterygoid fossa. A consultation with an infectious diseases specialist was sought.

A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A 52-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology in 2011 for a 2-month history of right-sided neck swelling, worsening dysphagia, and mild pain. Her past medical history was notable for excision of a dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the left inguinal–suprapubic region in 1998, with four local recurrences (2000, 2001, 2008, and 2009) treated surgically; she also received external radiotherapy (66 Gy) after the last excision.

On examination, there was a large, firm, mildly tender mass on the right side of the neck without fixation; the Pemberton sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed:
• TSH 0.363 mIU/L (0.32–5.0)  
• Free T4 14.6 pmol/L (9.0–19.0)  
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Intact PTH 6 pmol/L (1.48–8.43)

Ultrasound of the thyroid revealed a right lobe volume of 50 mL and left lobe 7.3 mL; the entire right lobe was replaced by a hypo- to anechoic mass measuring approximately 6 × 4 × 6 cm, displacing the trachea 1 cm to the left, with no pathological lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the right lobe yielded a hemorrhagic background with isolated clusters of pleomorphic round and oval nuclei; it was classified as category IV/3, suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax confirmed a voluminous right thyroid mass and detected two pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. MRI showed no lymphadenopathy. Laryngoscopy demonstrated freely mobile vocal cords.

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed macrophages 65.1%, lymphocytes 4.8%, neutrophils 29.9%, and eosinophils 0.2%, with no microorganisms or malignant cells. A 51-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of gradually progressive pain and swelling below his left knee, accompanied by intermittent fevers. Three months before presentation, the swelling ulcerated. He remained ambulatory without assistance.  
On examination, there was a firm mass measuring 30 × 18 × 12 cm over the distal tibia extending into the calf, with an anterior discharging ulcer 12 cm in diameter and areas of necrosis. The discharge was yellow and thick. Knee range of motion was reduced, and there was tenderness over the left knee and proximal tibia. Distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, popliteal) were intact and lower-limb neurologic examination was normal. Other systemic examination findings were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated a large metadiaphyseal lesion of the tibia with soft-tissue opacity, bone erosion and destruction of the tibia and adjacent fibula, and linear and ring-like calcifications, with extension into the proximal leg soft tissues. A Tc-99m bone scan revealed increased tracer uptake in the shaft of the left tibia and proximal soft tissue, without evidence of distant skeletal metastases. MRI was not obtained due to financial constraints.  
Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic appearance, the leading considerations were osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma of the tibia. On admission, the patient received intravenous antibiotics and analgesics and was counseled regarding treatment options. Taking into account lesion size, secondary infection, prosthesis cost, and prognosis, the patient elected transfemoral amputation with plans for postoperative chemotherapy.

A 62-year-old woman presented with 4 months of soreness, swelling, and limited movement of her right palm and wrist. Six months earlier, she had been stabbed by a fishbone. She had been diagnosed with a tenosynovial giant cell tumor by MRI at a local hospital and treated with traditional Chinese medicine, but her symptoms worsened over the past 2 months. She denied respiratory symptoms, skin disorders, recent travel, or tuberculosis exposure and had no family history of inflammatory arthritis or psoriasis. On examination, there was swelling, tenderness, and limited motion of the right palm and fingers without percussion pain or bone friction. Physiological reflexes were intact. Laboratory studies showed normal leukocyte count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; rheumatoid factor was negative. Noncontrast MRI of the right hand demonstrated patchy abnormal signal around the deep flexor tendons and carpal canal, with hypointense signals on T1-weighted imaging and hyperintense signals on proton-density fat-suppressed sequences. Post-contrast images demonstrated homogeneous enhancement of the tendons and synovial membrane, supporting synovial hyperplasia, while diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC maps suggested restricted diffusion. The median nerve was mildly compressed and deformed, and degenerative changes were noted in some carpal bones. Ultrasonography showed rough, thickened bone surfaces and decreased echogenicity at the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and along multiple flexor tendons, with peripheral and internal flow on color Doppler. The flexor retinaculum was elevated, and the median nerve was flattened at the carpal canal. Based on these findings, preliminary diagnoses included degenerative arthritis, synovitis, tenosynovitis, and atypical carpal tunnel syndrome; a neoplastic lesion remained in the differential.

A 72-year-old man with a history of stage IIIA gastric cancer treated by distal gastrectomy and adjuvant S-1 six months previously developed peritoneal and para-aortic lymph-node recurrence treated with weekly paclitaxel. After seven courses of chemotherapy, he experienced progressive anorexia and general fatigue and was referred for further evaluation.

On admission, he was alert. Temperature was 38.5 °C, blood pressure 110/53 mmHg, heart rate 64 beats/min, weight 60.2 kg (BMI 22.3 kg/m2). He had no skin or mucosal hyperpigmentation and normal pubic and axillary hair. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed: WBC 1.97×103/µL with neutrophils 350/µL, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, platelets 199×103/µL; CRP 3.1 mg/dL; blood glucose 101 mg/dL; electrolytes on admission normal (Na 141 mEq/L, K 4.1 mEq/L, Cl 101 mEq/L). CT scans showed no progression of lymph-node metastases or ascites, and no focus of infection.

One week after admission, his ECOG performance status declined from 2 to 4. On hospital day 5, laboratory tests revealed Na 122 mEq/L, serum osmolality 239 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 482 mOsm/kg. Fluid intake was restricted to 1 L/day for presumed SIADH, but the hyponatremia persisted.

An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative.

CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal.

Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension and Parkinson’s disease presented with 3 months of progressive lower extremity edema and acute onset of altered mental status. On admission, he was somnolent and disoriented; examination showed symmetric lower extremity edema, hepatomegaly, and ascites without stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests revealed AST 3877 U/L, ALT 2939 U/L, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, INR 3.8, white blood cell count 19.4×10^3/μL, platelets 63×10^3/μL, lactic acid 13.9 mmol/L, BUN 67 mg/dL, creatinine 3.3 mg/dL, with a negative acetaminophen level and toxicology screen. Viral hepatitis panels, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV testing were negative. A diagnostic paracentesis was negative for infection or malignancy. Tests for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, and Wilson’s disease were unremarkable. The patient developed hepatorenal syndrome requiring continuous venovenous hemofiltration.  
Lower-extremity Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral femoral–popliteal and iliac vein thrombosis. IVC filter placement was aborted due to clot burden. Hepatic ultrasonography with Doppler showed hepatic vein thrombosis and reversal of portal venous flow. Contrast CT of the abdomen, thorax, and pelvis revealed thrombus extending into the right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large echodense mass in the right atrium with preserved left ventricular function. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 10.6×5.0×5.6-cm heterogeneous pericardial mass invading the right atrium.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a facial angioma. MRI of the brain showed no leptomeningeal vascular malformations. Examination revealed bilateral naevus flammeus along the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve, more extensive on the right. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed iris heterochromia with diffuse hyperpigmentation and evenly distributed micronodular elevations on the iris surface. Intraocular pressure measured by Icare tonometry was 22 mm Hg in the right eye and 12 mm Hg in the left. Gonioscopy demonstrated open angles bilaterally with diffuse trabecular hyperpigmentation in the right eye. Anterior-segment OCT revealed increased reflectance of the iris surface in the right eye. Funduscopic examination showed increased retinal vessel tortuosity and a diffusely darker fundus in the right eye. B-scan ultrasonography measured choroidal thickness of 2.2 mm in the right eye versus 1.4 mm in the left. Macular spectral-domain OCT confirmed a thicker choroid in the right eye. Standard automated perimetry detected early visual-field defects in the right eye, and peripapillary OCT showed borderline retinal nerve-fibre-layer thickness on the right. Topical latanoprost was initiated in the right eye, reducing intraocular pressure to 17 mm Hg.

A 78-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, a history of moderately differentiated prostatic adenocarcinoma without evidence of metastasis, and nodular basal cell carcinoma presented with a lesion on the glans penis. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm irregular, friable mass on the glans. A deep shave biopsy showed nearly complete epidermal ulceration with replacement by an in-situ and diffusely infiltrative atypical clear cell tumor. Within the epidermis, the cells displayed diffuse pagetoid spread. The tumor consisted of large irregular nests and lobules of clear cells with abundant multivacuolated cytoplasm, nuclear indentations, and vesicular to hyperchromatic nuclei. Lymphovascular invasion was present. The initial differential diagnosis included a high-grade clear-cell squamous cell carcinoma and a metastatic clear-cell carcinoma.

A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

A 41-year-old man presented with a long-standing history of left plantar heel pain. Over two and a half years, he underwent extensive physiotherapy for presumed plantar fasciitis and tight gastrocnemius muscles, treatment with anti-inflammatory and analgesic medications, and two separate surgical releases (endoscopic plantar fascia release and minimally invasive gastrocnemius release) with only temporary relief. On re-presentation, he reported recurrent heel pain upon return to work.

On examination, he walked with an antalgic gait. The gastrocnemius remained tight with a positive Silfverskiöld test, and there was non-specific tenderness over the plantar aspect of the calcaneus at the insertion of the plantar fascia. 

Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral radiographs of the foot demonstrated normal bony relationships with no fractures, lesions, or signs of arthritis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot showed no thickening of the plantar fascia and no signal alteration in adjacent soft tissues or bone marrow. However, MRI revealed a pedunculated bony protrusion arising from the posterolateral plantar aspect of the calcaneus, measuring approximately 1.1 cm × 0.9 cm.

A 5-month-old dark-skinned boy was seen for evaluation of a congenital skin lesion on the left supraclavicular area. At birth, the lesion measured 11 cm × 3.5 cm; at 5 months it measured 10 cm × 2.5 cm. On examination, it was a single, nonpulsatile, well-demarcated, dark brown atrophic plaque with a linear midline depression and an elevated, compressible, soft border that was paler than the central portion. Birth and neonatal history were unremarkable; the patient was healthy and not on medications. The initial differential diagnosis included smooth muscle hamartoma, semiannular lipoatrophy, and, less likely, a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH). A small vein (~0.3 mm) was visible to the naked eye within the plaque. To avoid puncturing larger vessels during a planned biopsy, an AccuVein AV400 infrared vein finder was used; it revealed one large vein with an extensive network of small superficial branching vessels localized to the area of the atrophic plaque. A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

He reported fever and severe myalgia for 4 days, productive cough with yellow sputum but no hemoptysis, and 3 days of watery diarrhea. Chest radiograph and echocardiogram were unremarkable. A repeat abdominal ultrasound remained normal. Urinalysis showed no red cells, mild proteinuria, and 6–8 pus cells per high-power field. A 41-year-old woman with a 3-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presented with the sudden onset of visual disturbances. At the time of her SSc diagnosis, she had skin sclerosis of the fingers, hands, forearms, and face, Raynaud’s phenomenon with digital ulcers, multiple facial telangiectasias, esophageal reflux, and interstitial lung disease. Nail-fold capillaroscopy showed capillary loss with dilatation and microhemorrhages. A forearm skin biopsy demonstrated increased dermal collagen and superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Laboratory studies revealed a positive antinuclear antibody titer (>1:320) with a nucleolar pattern, negative anti-centromere antibody, and negative anti-Scl-70 antibody. She was treated with bosentan and aspirin, with stable pulmonary findings over two years.

Seven days before transfer, she was admitted elsewhere for fever over 38°C and headache. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 161.6 mg/dL, glucose 39 mg/dL, red blood cells 0 /mm3, and white blood cells 459 /mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear cells). Serum C-reactive protein was 10.6 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 82 mm/h. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions in the frontal, left parietal, and left occipital lobes with leptomeningeal enhancement. Empirical ceftriaxone and vancomycin were initiated. After four days, she developed visual disturbances; repeat MRI showed increased size and number of multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions along both cerebral hemispheres and midbrain, including a 4.5-cm lesion in the right posterior lobe. Tests of CSF—including Gram stain and culture, PCR for herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses, cryptococcal antigen, and fungal cultures—were negative. She was then referred to our hospital.

On arrival, she could only count fingers at close range and also reported headache, dizziness, fever, myalgia, polyarthralgia, and bilateral foot tingling. Blood pressure was 192/103 mmHg, heart rate 48 beats/min, and temperature 37.3°C. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia. Neurologic examination revealed drowsiness, neck stiffness, symmetrical proximal and distal weakness (muscle strength 4/5), paresthesia in both feet, brisk biceps reflexes, absent patellar reflexes, and bilaterally positive Babinski signs. A 4 × 5 cm ulcer was noted over the right lateral malleolus; there was no synovitis. The white-cell count was 14,090 /mm3, C-reactive protein was 3.09 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 56 mm/h. She continued antibiotics, and intravenous acyclovir, nicardipine, mannitol, and dexamethasone were added. Blood pressure stabilized within six hours, but her visual impairment worsened, and she developed left-sided weakness and new Raynaud’s phenomenon in her fingers. Emergent cerebral angiography revealed diffuse stenosis and a beaded pattern of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries and their branches, along with diffuse luminal narrowing and dysplastic changes in the right distal vertebral artery and basilar trunk, consistent with cerebral angiitis.

A 21-year-old woman presented with lifelong uncorrectable visual acuity and color vision impairment. There was no consanguinity in her family. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. She had myopia (–6.0 diopters) and intraocular pressures of 17 mmHg bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed thinning of the outer nuclear layer in the fovea, partial preservation of the ellipsoid zone, and a normal retinal nerve fiber layer. Full-field electroretinography (ff-ERG) revealed normal scotopic responses but attenuated photopic responses and 30-Hz flicker responses with delayed implicit times in both eyes.

He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

She was treated with calcitriol and phosphate and underwent percutaneous pinning of the femoral neck. She became pregnant; her phosphate and calcitriol were adjusted to maintain normal phosphorus levels, and genetic evaluation for hypophosphatemic disorders, including X-linked hypophosphatemia, was unremarkable. Family history was negative for bone disease. After a planned cesarean delivery, she continued to have disabling bilateral hip, knee, and ankle pain. On re-presentation, examination revealed a slow gait with a limp and lumbar tenderness. Current labs on calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and elemental phosphorus 500 mg twice daily included alkaline phosphatase 204 U/L, phosphorus 1.6 mg/dL, 25-OH vitamin D 32 ng/mL, 1,25[OH]2D3 32.4 pg/mL, calcium 9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and parathyroid hormone 74 pg/mL. Phosphate supplementation was increased to three times daily, raising the phosphorus level to 2.3 mg/dL. A gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/MRI showed a 9×8-mm intracortical lesion in the anterolateral right fibular head (standard uptake value [SUV], 65), with additional uptake in a right femoral neck stress fracture (SUV, 5.6) and bilateral calcaneal stress fractures (SUV, 4).

A 46-year-old woman presented with right flank pain, dysuria, and hematuria. Her past medical history was notable for an abdominal hysterectomy 15 years earlier. General and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Urinalysis showed 6–8 red blood cells and 4–6 pus cells per high-power field but no other abnormalities.

An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a focal hypoechoic polypoidal lesion measuring 3.4 × 2.8 cm along the anterosuperior wall of the urinary bladder, containing tiny hyperechoic foci; the outline of the adjacent bladder wall appeared indistinct. The uterus was not visualized; a cystic area was noted in the left adnexa, and both ovaries were not seen.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined soft-tissue–density lesion with calcific specks along the anterosuperior bladder wall that demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement in the early arterial and venous phases. The intraluminal component merged with the bladder wall, causing minimal localized wall thickening; the rest of the bladder wall was normal. Additional findings included a right calyceal calculus with mild pelvicalyceal dilatation, a simple right renal cyst, no pelvic lymphadenopathy, and left hydrosalpinx.

On imaging, possibilities such as endometriosis, a mucosal neoplastic lesion, or a granulomatous lesion of the urinary bladder were considered.

annotation_jobs.vignette:
An 82-year-old man with epithelioid pleural mesothelioma (cT1N0M0) was treated with ipilimumab and nivolumab. After eight courses, follow-up chest CT showed new bilateral infiltrative shadows. He reported fever and dyspnea. Laboratory tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein and surfactant protein D levels; Krebs von den Lungen-6 was normal. Sputum cultures, procalcitonin, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative. Serologic testing for anti–nuclear antigen, anti–aminoacyl–tRNA synthetase, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, anti-Sjögren’s-syndrome-related antigen A and B, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen antibodies were all negative. He had no history of antigen exposure. Immunotherapy was discontinued. He received lascufloxacin and then tazobactam/ceftolozane without improvement; oxygen requirement increased to 2 L/min. Based on the clinical picture and imaging, grade 3 ICI-induced pneumonitis was suspected. He underwent methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days followed by prednisolone 60 mg/day for 8 days, but chest radiographs remained unchanged and oxygen needs rose to 4 L/min. A second course of methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days produced no clinical improvement. One week later, bronchoscopy showed no airway secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 29% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 13% macrophages, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.33. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy, and cultures of bronchoscopy specimens were negative. Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with steroid-refractory ICI-induced pneumonitis.

A 76-year-old woman with a history of appendicitis, torsion of an ovarian cyst pedicle, and uterine myoma presented with a rapidly enlarging right parietal mass behind the ear over one month. She had no neurological deficits or systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies, including complete blood counts, metabolic panel, and viral serology for HIV and Epstein-Barr virus, were all normal or negative. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 5-cm hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the right parietal region. Cerebral angiography demonstrated a vascular tumor supplied by the middle meningeal artery. Thus, a clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made, and the differential diagnosis included primary lymphoma, metastasis, and sarcoma. The patient underwent endovascular embolization of the feeding artery followed by surgical resection. Intraoperatively, the tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement. Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm with positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin, and negative staining for Epstein-Barr virus.

During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

A 62-year-old man presented with a two-week history of an asymptomatic swelling in the right lower half of the face and reduced mouth opening. He reported two prior similar episodes over eight years: the first, five years ago, was treated as a buccal-space infection with incision and drainage; the second, two years ago, resolved spontaneously. He had no pain or fever and was a known diabetic on regular medication. 

On examination, there was gross right facial asymmetry. Extraorally, a 6 × 6 cm ovoid subcutaneous swelling extended from the level of the right lateral canthus to 1 cm below the corner of the mouth and from the corner of the mouth posteriorly to the mandibular ramus. The borders were ill-defined, the consistency ranged from soft to firm, and the overlying skin was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy, paresthesia, or facial palsy. Intraorally, the right buccal mucosa was elevated and glistening, with no vestibular obliteration; mouth opening was restricted by the mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the face showed a well-defined soft-tissue mass with cystic areas in the right buccal space. Intracystic loculations with dense cystic content were noted, and there was erosion of the posterior buccal cortex without perforation of the maxilla; the maxillary antrum was compressed.

A clinical diagnosis of a nonspecific chronic abscess with buccal-space involvement was made. Under general anesthesia, an intraoral approach was used to excise the lesion in toto with a margin of fibrous tissue. The lesion shelled out easily, with no involvement of buccinator muscle or bone. The excised specimen measured 4.8 × 4.5 cm, was creamish-brown, firm, irregular, and had a leathery pouch-like appearance, entirely within the soft tissue of the buccal space.

A 33-year-old Hispanic man with no known past medical history presented with a 1½-week history of headache and blurred vision. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.7-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with mass effect. He underwent craniotomy with biopsy and resection. Postoperatively, he was found to have HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 191 000 copies/mL. Serum toxoplasma IgG was elevated, and CSF studies showed 48 cells/µL (97% lymphocytes) with positive toxoplasma IgG and DNA-PCR for Toxoplasma gondii (286 copies/mL). Other CSF studies, including fungal cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and AFB smear/culture, were negative. Histopathologic examination of the brain tissue revealed bradyzoites and tachyzoites. He was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and started on antiretroviral therapy; empiric antibiotics for bacterial abscess were discontinued.

Two weeks after discharge, he returned with fever to 39.6 °C, generalized weakness, and a 1-day history of productive cough. Chest radiograph showed a new left upper lobe opacification with diffuse reticulonodular interstitial prominence. CT scan of the chest confirmed extensive reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates with focal consolidation in the left upper lobe. He was started on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and fluconazole and placed on airborne precautions. His respiratory status worsened, and intubation was planned pending further diagnostic evaluation.

A 42-year-old man with 30 pack-years of smoking, cannabis use, alcohol dependence, and the use of herbal products for addiction cessation presented with a 3-day history of acute urinary retention, hematemesis, and progressive neurological deficits. On day 3, he developed marked paraparesis of the lower limbs (muscle strength 2/5), was unable to stand or walk, and had hyperreflexia with sustained clonus in the lower extremities. Sensory function—including proprioception, light touch, and vibration—was normal. He also had hypertonic sphincters and hyperalgesia. Cranial nerve and upper limb examinations were normal. He was febrile, and his condition deteriorated into respiratory distress requiring intubation and sedation.

Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid without albuminocytologic dissociation: glucose 0.49 g/L, protein 0.20 g/L, chloride 121 mmol/L, 14 white blood cells (70% lymphocytes), and 14 red blood cells per mm³; cultures were sterile. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL falling to 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (18 350 cells/μL), platelet counts fluctuating between 98 000 and 136 000 cells/μL, hyponatremia corrected from 117.5 mEq/L to 146 mEq/L over 8 days, potassium levels between 5.5 and 4.6 mEq/L, elevated AST (134 U/L) and ALT (65.9 U/L), and CRP 128.8–131.2 mg/L. Renal function remained normal.

Initial brain MRI showed multiple bilateral, symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and periaqueductal regions, dorsomedial thalami, medial temporal lobes, caudate nuclei, and brainstem, with diffusion restriction and low ADC values. Spinal MRI demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensities throughout the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar cord. A follow-up MRI a few days later revealed worsening of these lesions, new involvement of the lenticular nuclei, and patchy contrast enhancement in the cerebral peduncles, superior cerebellar peduncles, superior colliculi, right pons, and bilateral medulla. There was more extensive bilateral FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter and progression of the spinal cord lesions.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed lymphadenopathy in the bilateral cervical and axillary regions, left inguinal lymphadenopathy, and marked peri- and pararenal soft-tissue infiltration.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of abnormal behavior, decreased concentration, and postural instability. She had a history of insomnia and irritable bowel syndrome and was taking vitamin D3, vitamin K, manganese, and activated charcoal. She and her parents denied other medications. She had been started on lorazepam by her general practitioner without improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Teeth had a greyish discoloration. Neurologic exam showed confusion, impaired attention, and disorientation. Muscle tone and strength were normal; coordination, sensation, and cranial nerves were intact; there were no pyramidal signs.

While in the emergency department, she became more somnolent and developed frequent myoclonic jerks. Laboratory tests including CBC, renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, CRP, vitamin B12, and folate were normal; syphilis and HIV tests were negative. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed protein 47 mg/dL (15–45) and 10 WBC/μL (<5). Empiric IV acyclovir and ceftriaxone were started for possible infectious encephalitis.

On the neurology service, she remained moderately drowsy with exuberant generalized myoclonus at rest and on action. EEG revealed generalized background slowing without focal or periodic features. Brain MRI on hospital day 5 was normal. She clinically worsened despite antivirals and antibiotics, so intravenous immunoglobulin was given empirically for presumed autoimmune encephalitis. A trial of levetiracetam 1000 mg/day failed to improve the myoclonus.

A 34‐year‐old woman presented with pain and slight mobility of the mandibular right second premolar and first molar. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, percussion of both teeth was tender, and slight mobility was noted, but the overlying mucosa and skin were normal with no erythema, ulceration, or warmth. Intraoral palpation revealed bony‐hard consistency of the buccal and lingual cortices, and the mucosal integrity was intact.

An initial orthopantomogram showed a unilocular radiolucent lesion engulfing the apices of the right mandibular second premolar and a previously endodontically treated first molar, extending to the superior border of the inferior alveolar nerve canal; its irregular shape was atypical for routine periapical cysts or granulomas. Cone beam CT further demonstrated buccolingual expansion with almost complete obliteration of the lingual cortex, measuring approximately 23.4 × 14.2 × 6.6 mm.

Based on the radiographic findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, radicular cyst, and unicystic ameloblastoma.

A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. He denied contact allergens, fever, or hyperhidrosis and had no prior history of atopic dermatitis, dermatophytosis, or hand eczema. On examination, he had scleral icterus and multiple dusky, thin plaques with a central collarette of scale on the face, neck, axillae, trunk, and extremities. On both hands and feet, there were hyperkeratotic plaques and deeply seated vesicles with a greenish-black hue, especially accentuated along the dermatoglyphic ridges. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. A punch biopsy of the right palm revealed psoriasiform epidermal acanthosis, intraepidermal spongiosis, hyperkeratosis with sparse perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and a dilated eccrine duct containing amorphous pink material. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

A 10-day-old, 40-kg male Chianina calf was referred for evaluation of progressive dyspnea, lethargy, and recumbency. On presentation, temperature was 38.5 °C; heart rate, 170 beats/min with regular rhythm; respiratory rate, 60 breaths/min; jugular pulses were present and mucous membranes were cyanotic, especially after brief exertion. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade IV/VI right apical systolic murmur and a more pronounced heartbeat on the right precordium. Lung sounds were harsh bronchovesicular. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 170 beats/min. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle, a markedly hypoplastic left ventricle with a severely reduced mitral valve orifice, a 16 mm interatrial defect in the upper septum, and a 6 mm muscular interventricular defect in the dorsal septum. An oblique parasternal long-axis view revealed two great vessels arising in parallel from the right ventricle, differentiated by coronary arteries from one vessel and by left and right pulmonary arteries from the other. Color-flow Doppler showed severe tricuspid regurgitation and bidirectional shunting at both septal defects. Agitated saline contrast injected via the left jugular vein produced bubbles in the left atrium and ventricle and exiting the right ventricle through both great vessels.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painless mass on the right side of the frontal bone. On examination, the mass measured approximately 4.0 × 3.5 cm, was well circumscribed, soft, nonmobile, and non-tender. Laboratory studies and neurologic examination were unremarkable.

Plain radiography of the skull showed a large, circumscribed radiolucent lesion in the right frontal bone without adjacent soft-tissue swelling. CT of the head demonstrated a lytic lesion of the frontal bone with a soap-bubble appearance, cortical destruction of the inner and outer tables, and an associated soft-tissue component. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a lobulated frontal-bone mass measuring 3.7 × 3.3 × 2.8 cm that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed avid enhancement on postcontrast sequences.

A 30-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, calcified mass on the right anterior maxilla that had been present for 18 months. On intraoral examination, there was a mucosal fenestration through which a hard, mineralized structure approximately 1 cm in diameter was visible. A periapical radiograph of the upper right premolar area demonstrated a discrete radiopaque lesion. The initial diagnostic hypothesis was maxillary exostosis. An incisional biopsy was performed to remove a fragment of the lesion, which was submitted for histopathological analysis.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology.

Laboratory studies, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125, were all within normal limits; the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) score was 4.1 %. Serological testing for Echinococcus granulosus was negative. A giant intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed preoperatively, and laparoscopic cyst aspiration with exploration under general anesthesia was planned.
